newsitem.title: JAPAN: STOCKS-Asian markets bruised by Wall Street tumble.
newsitem.headline: STOCKS-Asian markets bruised by Wall Street tumble.

text.p: Stock markets across Asia came up bruised on Friday after Wall Street took a tumble, with Tokyo's Nikkei average falling more than one percent.

In early afternoon trade, Tokyo's benchmark 225-share Nikkei average had fallen 268.59 points, or 1.31 percent, to 20,284.39, after cracking under the weight of uncertainties about the economy as well as a sharp fall on Wall Street overnight, brokers said.
Sydney and Wellington were also off in late afternoon trade, as were Hong Kong and Singapore, but Taipei was flat as investors there looked more for factors from China than the United States.

In New York, blue-chip stocks sank to their biggest loss since mid-July on Thursday as fresh signs of a surprisingly strong economy boosted long-term bond interest rates above seven percent. The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 64.73
points at 5,647.65, its largest drop since July 15, when it closed with a loss of 161 points.
Tokyo was one of the hardest hit Asian markets, with investors still worried about a survey released on Wednesday which showed worse-than-expected confidence in the economy.
"The fundamentals were bad to begin with due to the Bank of Japan survey and then the New York market fell on top of that," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities.
New Zealand recovered by the close, ending down 10.77 points, or 0.48 percent, at 2228.77 after losing more than 16 points in earlier trade.
"...The market has seen some very, very good days, so it's probably overdue for a breather," said Ord Minnett director John Rattray.

Sydney's All Ordinaries index had also recovered slightly from the Dow's fall by late afternoon trade. The index was down 9.3 points, or 0.41 percent, to 2270.0 after dropping almost 15 points in the morning.
Brokers said Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was also pulled down by New York.
In late morning trade it was down 154 points, or 1.36 percent, to 11,174.
"It's just in line with the Dow Jones," said Priscilla Ng, executive director at CEF Brokerage. "I think it is just an excuse to sell down the market."

The Weighted Index in Taiwan was down 2.61 points, or just 0.04 percent, to 6309.82 by midday as comments by Chinese President Jiang Zemin that political differences would not interfere with Taiwan-China economic ties overrode the Dow's fall.
Singapore also fell in line with New York, with the Straits Times Industrials index falling 19.82 points, or 0.92 percent, to 2142.83.
